title: The Boat That Knew the Way
blurb: Mateo sails with his grandfather and learns to read the water.
pages: Mateo woke before the sun.
The house was dark and quiet.
Down at the shore, his grandfather was already loading the boat.
It was a long wooden boat with a wing on each side.
Lolo called those wings outriggers.
They kept the boat from tipping over.
"Are you coming?"
Lolo asked.
Mateo pulled on his sandals and ran.
The sand was still cold.
The water was flat and grey.
Mateo climbed in and sat where he always sat, right behind his grandfather.
Lolo pushed off.
The boat slid away from the beach without a sound.
Mateo watched the shore get smaller.
Soon the houses looked like little boxes.
"How do you know where to go?"
Mateo asked.
There were no signs out here.
There were no roads.
Lolo did not answer right away.
He looked at the water for a long moment.
Then he said, "The boat knows.
And the water tells you, if you learn how to listen."
Mateo did not understand.
Not yet.
The sun came up behind them.
It turned the water orange, then gold, then blue.
Mateo leaned over the side and looked down.
He could see all the way to the bottom.
There were rocks down there, and grass that waved back and forth.
A small fish darted under the boat and disappeared.
"Shallow here,"
said Lolo.
"See how the water is bright?
Bright means the bottom is close."
Mateo looked again.
The bright part went on and on, and then it stopped, and everything past it was dark.
"What about the dark part?"
Mateo asked.
"Deep,"
said Lolo.
"That is where we are going."
He turned the boat, and they crossed the line where bright became dark.
Mateo felt something change.
The boat rocked differently.
The waves were slower here, and taller, and they lifted the whole boat up and set it down again.
It was not scary.
It was like being rocked.
Mateo let go of the side and put his hands in his lap.
Lolo cut the engine.
The quiet was enormous.
Mateo could hear water tapping the side of the boat and nothing else.
No cars.
No television.
No one calling his name.
Lolo handed him a line with a hook on the end.
"Drop it,"
he said.
"Then wait."
Mateo dropped it.
The line went down and down and kept going.
He waited.
Nothing happened.
He waited some more.
Waiting, it turned out, was most of fishing.
After a while Mateo got bored.
He wiggled.
He tapped his foot on the bottom of the boat.
Lolo did not say stop.
He just said, "The fish can feel that."
Mateo froze.
"They can feel my foot?"
"They feel everything,"
said Lolo.
"Sound travels better in water than in air."
Mateo held very still.
It was hard.
His leg wanted to move.
But he held still, and he listened, and slowly the boat and the water and his own breathing all seemed to line up.
The line jerked.
Mateo grabbed it with both hands.
"Pull steady,"
said Lolo.
"Not fast.
Steady."
Mateo pulled.
Whatever was down there pulled back.
His arms burned.
He wanted to yank as hard as he could, but he remembered what Lolo said, and he kept pulling the same slow way.
Hand over hand.
The line came up wet and cold.
Then a flash of silver came up under the water, turning and turning, getting bigger.
The fish came over the side and landed in the boat.
It was longer than Mateo's arm.
Its scales were silver and blue and they caught the light.
It flapped once, hard, and Mateo jumped back.
Lolo laughed.
It was the first time Mateo had heard him laugh all morning.
"That is a good fish,"
Lolo said.
"That is dinner and lunch tomorrow."
Mateo could not stop grinning.
His arms were shaking and he did not care at all.
On the way back, Mateo watched the water again.
This time he noticed things.
He noticed where it went bright.
He noticed a patch that was darker than the rest, and he pointed at it.
"Deep?"
he asked.
Lolo nodded.
"Deep.
Or a cloud is over it.
You have to look up too."
Mateo looked up.
There was a cloud, right above the dark patch, exactly where Lolo said it would be.
Mateo felt very pleased with himself.
The shore came back.
The little boxes turned into houses again.
Lolo let Mateo steer the last part, with one hand on the boat behind him just in case.
"You said the boat knows the way,"
Mateo said.
"Does it really?"
Lolo shrugged.
"My father said it to me.
I think what he meant is that if you go out enough times, you stop needing to be told."
Mateo nodded slowly.
He thought he understood now.
Next week, he would look at the water first, before anyone told him anything.

checks.q: Why do the outriggers matter?
o: They keep the boat from tipping over
They make the boat go faster
checks.why: Page 1 says it straight out: the wings kept the boat from tipping over.

checks.q: How can Mateo tell the water is shallow?
checks.why: Lolo teaches him that bright water means the bottom is close. Dark means deep.

checks.q: Why does Mateo stop moving his foot?
o: Lolo told him the fish can feel it
checks.why: Cause and effect. Lolo says the fish feel everything, so Mateo holds still.

checks.q: What does Lolo mean by "pull steady"?
o: Pull as hard as you can
Pull the same slow way, over and over
checks.why: Mateo wants to yank hard, but he keeps pulling the same slow way instead. Hand over hand.

checks.q: What has changed about Mateo by the end?
o: He starts noticing the water himself
checks.why: At the start he asked how Lolo knew. At the end he spots the dark patch before being told.

checks.q: What is this story mostly about?
o: A boy learning to read the water
checks.why: Main idea. Every part is about Mateo learning to see what Lolo sees.

words: The wings on each side of the boat that keep it from tipping.
Very, very big. The quiet was enormous means it filled everything.
Went out of sight. Dis- at the front means the opposite, so it un-appeared.
Even and the same, not jerky. Steady pulling, not fast pulling.
Not deep. You can see the bottom.

title: The Robot That Would Not Charge
blurb: Ivy has one afternoon to fix a robot before the science fair.
pages: Ivy had built the robot out of a shoebox, four bottle caps, and a small motor from a broken fan.
She had named it Bolt.
Bolt could drive forward.
Bolt could turn left.
Bolt could not turn right, but Ivy figured nobody would ask.
The science fair was tomorrow at nine in the morning.
Ivy plugged Bolt into the charger and went to eat dinner.
When she came back, the little light on Bolt's side was still dark.
Ivy unplugged the charger and plugged it back in.
Nothing.
She wiggled the cord.
Nothing.
She turned Bolt over and looked at the bottom, which was mostly tape.
Everything looked the way it had looked yesterday, when it worked.
"Come on,"
she said out loud.
Bolt said nothing back, because Bolt was a shoebox.
Ivy sat down on the floor and put her chin in her hands and stared at it.
Her brother Marcus walked past with a bowl of cereal.
"Is it broken?"
he asked.
"It's not broken,"
Ivy said.
"It just won't charge."
Marcus took a loud bite.
"That's broken."
Ivy did not answer.
Marcus leaned in the doorway and chewed.
Then he said, "When Dad's drill won't charge, he checks the outlet first.
Sometimes it's not the drill."
He walked away.
Ivy sat there for a second.
Then she got up.
She plugged a lamp into the outlet behind her desk.
The lamp came on.
So the outlet worked.
That meant the problem was somewhere between the outlet and Bolt.
Ivy felt a small spark of excitement.
This was like the mystery books she liked, where you cross things off a list until only one thing is left.
She got a piece of paper and wrote at the top: WHAT IS BROKEN.
Then she wrote: outlet — NO.
Next she tested the charger.
She had another gadget that used the same kind of plug, an old music player.
She plugged the charger into the music player.
A little battery symbol appeared on its screen.
The charger worked too.
Ivy wrote: charger — NO.
Two things crossed off.
She looked at Bolt sitting on the carpet with its bottle-cap wheels.
"So it is you,"
she said.
Bolt, once again, said nothing.
Ivy peeled back the tape on Bolt's bottom, one strip at a time, so she could put it back the same way.
Inside were the motor, the battery, and a tangle of wires she had twisted together herself last week.
She looked at them closely.
One of the wires was not touching anything.
Its end had slipped out from under the tape and was just floating there, going nowhere.
Ivy stared at it.
That was it.
That was the whole problem.
She twisted the loose wire back onto the little metal post where it belonged.
Then she taped it down, and then, because she had learned something, she taped it down a second time in the other direction.
She plugged Bolt in.
The light on Bolt's side turned orange.
Ivy shouted so loudly that Marcus yelled "WHAT"
from the other room.
"NOTHING,"
Ivy yelled back, grinning at the little orange light.
While Bolt charged, Ivy thought about the loose wire.
Why had it come loose?
She had twisted it on tight.
But she had also carried Bolt to school in her backpack on Friday, and the backpack had been thrown around a lot.
That was probably it.
Movement.
She wrote on her paper: TAPE EVERYTHING TWICE.
Then she added: CHECK THE OUTLET FIRST.
She was starting to like this list.
In the morning, Bolt drove across the gym floor in front of three judges.
It went forward.
It turned left.
One judge asked, "Can it turn right?"
Ivy took a breath.
"Not yet,"
she said.
"The motor on that side is from a fan and it only spins one way.
I'd need a different motor."
The judge wrote something down.
Ivy could not tell if it was good or bad.
She did not win first place.
She won a small green ribbon that said PROBLEM SOLVING.
Ivy thought that was funny, because the part she was proudest of was not building Bolt at all.
It was the piece of paper with things crossed off it.
On the way home she asked Marcus how he knew about the outlet.
He shrugged.
"Dad told me.
He said start with the easy stuff."
Ivy decided that was the best advice she had ever gotten.

checks.q: What is Ivy's problem at the start?
checks.why: The light stays dark after she plugs Bolt in. That is the problem she has to solve.

checks.q: What does Marcus suggest?
checks.why: He says when Dad's drill won't charge, he checks the outlet first — sometimes it isn't the drill.

checks.q: Why does Ivy test the lamp and the music player?
o: To cross things off and narrow it down
checks.why: She's crossing things off a list until only one thing is left, like in her mystery books.

checks.q: What was actually wrong with Bolt?
checks.why: One wire had slipped out from under the tape and wasn't touching anything.

checks.q: Why does Ivy write TAPE EVERYTHING TWICE?
o: So it won't shake loose in her backpack again
checks.why: She works out that the backpack getting thrown around shook the wire loose.

checks.q: Why is Ivy proudest of the piece of paper?
o: It shows how she figured the problem out
It had her name on it
checks.why: Inference. The ribbon says PROBLEM SOLVING, and the list is the record of her solving it.

words: The thing that puts power back into a battery. Charge plus -er means the thing that charges.
The feeling of being excited. Excite plus -ment turns it into a thing you feel.
Most likely, but not for sure.
People who decide who wins. The g sounds like a j.

title: The Dog Who Could Count
blurb: Nobody believes Sam until they see it for themselves.
pages: Sam's dog was named Waffle.
Waffle was mostly brown, with one white ear that stuck up and one that flopped down.
Waffle could not do any tricks.
He could not sit on command.
He could not roll over.
If you threw a ball, Waffle would watch it go, and then look at you like you had made a mistake.
Sam loved him anyway.
But Sam had noticed something about Waffle that nobody else had, and it was starting to bother him.
It started with the treats.
Sam kept them in a jar on the counter.
Every afternoon he gave Waffle three.
One, two, three, and then Sam would put the lid back on.
Waffle would eat all three and walk away.
But one day Sam was in a hurry and only gave him two.
Waffle did not walk away.
He sat down in front of the counter and stared at the jar and would not move.
Sam gave him the third one.
Then Waffle left.
Sam thought that was a coincidence.
So the next day he tried it on purpose.
Two treats.
Waffle sat and stared.
Three treats.
Waffle left.
Four treats, just to see.
Waffle ate all four and left, looking pleased.
Sam wrote it all down in the back of his math notebook.
Two: waits.
Three: leaves.
Four: leaves.
It looked like Waffle knew when three had happened.
Sam told his sister Priya.
Priya was eleven and did not believe anything.
"Dogs can't count,"
she said, without looking up from her book.
"He knows,"
said Sam.
"He waits when it's two."
"He's just hungry,"
said Priya.
"He's always hungry."
"Then why does he leave at three?"
Priya turned a page.
"Because he's full."
"He's not full after three tiny treats!"
Priya did not answer.
Sam went to find a better experiment.
Here was the problem.
If Waffle only left when he was full, then bigger treats should make him leave sooner.
So Sam broke the treats in half.
He gave Waffle three halves, which is less food than two whole ones.
Waffle ate all three halves and walked away.
Sam felt a jolt go through him.
It was not about how much.
It was about how many.
He wrote it down twice so he would not lose it.
He showed Priya the notebook.
She read it.
Then she read it again.
Then she put her book face down on the table, which was the most attention Sam had gotten from her in a month.
"Do it in front of me,"
she said.
So they went to the kitchen.
Sam got the jar.
Waffle came trotting in with his one ear up and one ear down, and sat down on the tile, and waited.
Sam gave him one half.
Waffle ate it and stayed.
Two halves.
Waffle ate it and stayed, watching the jar.
Priya crossed her arms.
Three halves.
Waffle chewed, licked his nose, stood up, and walked out of the kitchen without looking back.
Priya said a word she was not supposed to say.
Then she said, "Do it again."
They did it four more times.
It worked four more times.
Priya got very serious.
She said real scientists have to try to prove themselves wrong, not right.
So they tested it a different way.
Priya held the treats and Sam left the room, in case Sam was giving Waffle some secret signal without knowing it.
It still worked.
Then they tried the whole thing in the living room instead of the kitchen, in case it was the tile.
It still worked.
Waffle stopped at three every single time.
They never did figure out how.

Priya's guess was that Waffle was not counting the way people count, with numbers, but that three had become a shape to him, the way a song feels finished at the end even if you are not counting the notes.
Sam liked that idea.
He liked it better than numbers.
He wrote it in the notebook under everything else, in his best handwriting.
At dinner Sam told his parents, and his dad laughed and said sure, and his mom said that's nice honey.
Neither of them got up to look.
Sam did not mind as much as he thought he would.
He and Priya knew.
The notebook knew.
And Waffle, who could not sit, could not roll over, and could not fetch a ball to save his life, sat under the table with his one ear up, waiting for exactly three more.

checks.q: What does Waffle do when Sam gives him only two treats?
o: He sits and stares at the jar
checks.why: That's the clue that starts the whole story — at two he refuses to leave.

checks.q: Why does Sam try it again the next day on purpose?
o: To check whether the first time was just chance
checks.why: He thought it was a coincidence, so he tested it deliberately. That's what makes it an experiment.

checks.q: What is Priya's explanation?
checks.why: She argues he leaves because he's full, not because he counted.

checks.q: How does breaking the treats in half prove Priya wrong?
o: Three halves is less food, and he still left
checks.why: Three halves is less food than two wholes. If it were about being full he'd have stayed.

checks.q: Why does Sam leave the room during one test?
o: In case he was giving Waffle a signal without meaning to
checks.why: Priya says scientists try to prove themselves wrong. Removing Sam removes one explanation.

checks.q: What is Priya's guess about how Waffle does it?
o: He uses numbers like people do
Three feels like a finished shape to him
checks.why: She compares it to a song feeling finished, even if you aren't counting notes.

words: When two things happen together by chance, not because one caused the other.
A test you set up carefully to find out if something is true.
People whose job is figuring out how things work. The sci- sounds like sigh.
Looking at something and thinking about it.
The way you write letters with your hand. Two words stuck together.

title: Lost on the Fourth Floor
blurb: Nadia gets separated from her mother and has to think.
pages: Nadia was looking at a display of snow globes when she realized her mother was gone.
She turned around and there was just a rack of coats, and past that, strangers.
Nadia's stomach went cold.
She had been standing right there.
Her mother had said, "Stay close,"
and Nadia had said, "Okay,"
and then there had been the snow globes, and then this.
She was eight years old and she was by herself on the fourth floor of a very large store.
Her first thought was to run.
Just start moving and looking.
She actually took two steps before she stopped.
She stopped because she remembered something her mother had told her once in the car, in a bored voice, the way you say a thing you do not expect to need.
If you get lost, do not go looking.
Looking makes it worse, because now two people are moving.
Stay where you are.
Nadia planted her feet.
Standing still was much harder than she expected.
Every second felt long.
People walked past her and none of them were her mother.
A woman with a stroller.
A man carrying a lamp.
Two teenagers laughing at something on a phone.
Nadia counted her breaths to keep from crying, which was something else her mother had taught her, and got to forty-one before it started to work.
After a few minutes, Nadia thought about it more carefully.
Staying put only works if the other person knows where to look.
Her mother knew Nadia had been at the snow globes.
So the snow globes were the right place to be.
Nadia moved back until she was standing exactly next to the display, close enough to touch it.
Now she was not just standing still.
She was standing still in the correct spot.
That felt different.
That felt like a decision.
The next question was harder.
What if her mother was on a different floor?
What if she had gone down the escalator without noticing?
Nadia looked around for someone who worked there.
She had been told about this too: find a worker, or a parent with children, and do not go anywhere with anyone.
There was a woman folding sweaters twenty steps away with a name tag on her shirt.
Nadia walked the twenty steps.
"Excuse me,"
Nadia said.
Her voice came out much smaller than she meant it to.
The woman looked up.
"I can't find my mom."
The woman put the sweater down immediately.
She did not look annoyed.
She crouched down so her face was level with Nadia's.
"Okay,"
she said.
"That's okay.
What is your mom's name?"
Nadia told her.
The woman said, "And what's your name?"
Nadia told her that too.
Her voice was steadier the second time.
The woman, whose name tag said RITA, picked up a small radio from her belt.
She said Nadia's mother's name into it, and the words carried out into the whole store, in every direction, on every floor.
Nadia had not thought of that.
She had been trying to solve it with her feet.
Rita had solved it with her voice.
Rita said, "Now we wait right here, so she knows where to come."
That was the same rule Nadia had figured out.
They waited by the snow globes.

Rita asked Nadia which one she liked best, and Nadia pointed at one with a lighthouse in it, and Rita said that was the good one, obviously, and Nadia laughed a little even though her eyes were still wet.
It had been about six minutes.
It had felt like an hour and a half.
Then Nadia heard footsteps that were faster than everyone else's, and her mother came around the coat rack with her face completely white.
She hugged Nadia so hard it hurt.
"I turned around,"
her mother kept saying, "I turned around for one second."
Nadia said, "I stayed where I was."
Her mother pulled back and looked at her.
"You did?"
"You told me to,"
Nadia said.
Her mother started to cry, which was very strange to watch.
In the car, her mother said, "I am so proud of you."
Nadia looked out the window.
She did not feel brave.
She had been terrified the whole time.
But she thought maybe that was what it actually was — not the absence of being scared, but doing the sensible thing anyway while your stomach was cold and your hands would not stay still.
She decided she liked that better.
It meant she could do it again.

checks.q: Why does Nadia decide not to run and look?
o: If both people move, it takes longer to find each other
A worker told her not to
checks.why: Her mother's rule: looking makes it worse because now two people are moving.

checks.q: Why does Nadia move back to the snow globes?
o: It's the last place her mother saw her
checks.why: Staying put only works if the other person knows where to look — so she stands where she was last seen.

checks.q: Who does Nadia decide to ask for help?
o: A worker with a name tag
checks.why: The rule she was taught: find a worker, or a parent with children, and don't go anywhere with anyone.

checks.q: How does Rita solve the problem differently than Nadia was trying to?
o: She uses the radio to reach the whole store
checks.why: Nadia was trying to solve it with her feet. Rita solves it with her voice, over the radio.

checks.q: Why does Nadia's mother start to cry?
o: She is relieved, and proud that Nadia did the right thing
checks.why: Inference. Her face was white with fear, and she cries after finding Nadia safe and hearing she stayed put.

checks.q: What does Nadia decide bravery actually is?
o: Doing the sensible thing even while you are scared
checks.why: She says it's not the absence of being scared — it's doing the sensible thing anyway.

words: The moving stairs in a store.
Smart and reasonable. The sensible thing is the thing that makes good sense.

title: Nobody Beats the Tower
blurb: Kai has climbed the tower nine hundred times. Tonight he brings a stranger.
pages: The tower was made of blocks and it went up forever.
Kai had been climbing it for four months.
He had gotten to the ledge with the spinning arms.
He had gotten past the part where the floor disappears if you stand still.
He had never once gotten to the top.
Nobody had.
There was a leaderboard at the bottom of the tower and the top name had been the same for a year: a player called MOSSGIRL, stuck at ninety-four percent.
Kai's avatar was a blocky little guy with a green headband.
He had spent all his coins on that headband and no coins at all on anything useful.
He liked how it looked when he jumped.
Tonight he was on section eleven, the one with the moving platforms, and he had fallen off it eleven times in a row, which felt like the tower making fun of him.
He fell a twelfth time.
The screen went grey and dropped him back at the bottom.
Kai made a noise into his headset that was mostly frustration.
Then a message popped up in the corner.
MOSSGIRL: you keep jumping too early.
Kai stared at it.
MOSSGIRL was here?
At the bottom?
MOSSGIRL: watch the third platform not the second one.
Kai typed back: why are you down here.
MOSSGIRL: because I got stuck for a year and I got bored of being stuck.
They climbed together.
It was slower with two people, because you had to wait, and Kai was bad at waiting.
But MOSSGIRL kept saying things that turned out to be right.
Look where you're going to land, not where you are.
Don't sprint into a jump you haven't measured.
If you fall the same way twice, the problem isn't the tower.
Kai found that last one annoying, mostly because it was true.
Section eleven again.
Kai stood on the ledge and watched the platforms swing past.
Before, he had always jumped at the first gap he saw, because waiting made him itchy.
This time he counted.
One swing.
Two swings.
On the third, the far platform came close enough that the gap was almost nothing.
He jumped and landed with room to spare.
It was so easy it was almost insulting.
MOSSGIRL: told you.
Section twelve was a wall of blocks that fell away one at a time.
Section thirteen was dark and you had to remember the path from the flash of light every few seconds.
Kai's hands hurt.
He had been playing for an hour and forty minutes and he had completely forgotten to be bored, which almost never happened to him.
He looked at the little percentage in the corner.
Sixty-one.
Then sixty-eight.
Then seventy-three.
At eighty-nine percent MOSSGIRL stopped.
Kai turned his avatar around.
She was standing on the last solid platform, not moving.
MOSSGIRL: this is where I always quit.
Kai typed: why.
There was a long pause.
MOSSGIRL: because the next part you can't practice.
you get one try and if you miss you go all the way back to the bottom.
Kai looked up at the next part.
It was a single long jump across nothing.
Kai thought about the bottom.
Four months of the bottom.
Then he thought about something his mom said when he did not want to start his homework, which was that the worst part is almost always the ten seconds before you start.
He typed: on three.
MOSSGIRL: seriously?
Kai typed: 1.
Kai typed: 2.
He did not type 3.
He just ran, because he knew if he waited he would talk himself out of it.
He missed.
He fell the whole way down, past section thirteen, past the swinging platforms, past the ledge with the spinning arms, all the way to the grass at the bottom where he had started four months ago.
The screen said 0%.
Kai sat back in his chair and laughed out loud, alone in his room, because it had been so completely worth it and he could not explain why.
A message came in.
MOSSGIRL: I did it.
MOSSGIRL: I went right after you.
MOSSGIRL: I've been standing on that ledge for a YEAR.
Then a second later: MOSSGIRL: get back up here.
Kai looked at the tower going up and up out of sight.
Ninety-four percent had been the top of the leaderboard for a year, and now it was not, and the reason was that somebody had gone first and missed.
Kai started climbing.

checks.q: What is Kai's problem on section eleven?
checks.why: MOSSGIRL tells him straight away: he keeps jumping too early and should watch the third platform.

checks.q: What does "if you fall the same way twice, the problem isn't the tower" mean?
o: He needs to change what he's doing
checks.why: It means the repeat isn't bad luck — it's something in how he's playing. Kai finds it annoying because it's true.

checks.q: How does Kai finally clear section eleven?
o: He counts the swings and waits for the third
checks.why: He counts one swing, two swings, and jumps on the third when the gap is almost nothing.

checks.q: Why has MOSSGIRL been stuck for a year?
o: The next jump gives you one try, and missing sends you to the bottom
checks.why: She says you can't practice it — one try, and a miss costs the whole climb.

checks.q: Why does Kai run without typing 3?
o: If he waited he would talk himself out of it
He wanted to win the race
checks.why: He remembers that the worst part is the ten seconds before you start, so he removes those seconds.

checks.q: Why does Kai laugh after falling all the way down?
o: He thought it was funny that he lost
Trying the jump was worth it even though he missed
checks.why: Inference. He says it was completely worth it and he can't explain why — the attempt mattered more than the result.

words: A list showing who is doing best.
The feeling when you keep trying and it keeps not working.
Flat surfaces you stand or jump on.
Rude — as if it were making fun of you.
How much of the whole you have done, out of a hundred.

title: The Substitute
blurb: Mr. Ballard is either the best teacher ever or a complete disaster.
pages: The note on the whiteboard said MRS.
OKAFOR IS OUT TODAY.
Under it, in enormous letters that went off the edge of the board, somebody had written: I AM MR.
BALLARD.
The man at the desk was wearing a tie with pineapples on it.
He had his feet up.
When the bell rang he stood so fast his chair fell over backwards, and he did not pick it up.
"GOOD MORNING,"
he said, much too loudly.
Half the class jumped.
"Here is what I know,"
said Mr.
Ballard.
"You have math at nine.
You have reading at ten.
I have been given a folder."
He held up a folder.
"I have not read it."
Somebody laughed.
Mr.
Ballard looked delighted.
"I am going to read it now, out loud, at the same time as you, and we will find out together what we are supposed to be doing."
Malia, who liked things to go normally, felt her stomach tighten.
The folder said: MULTIPLICATION REVIEW, PAGES 40 TO 42.
"Ugh,"
said Mr.
Ballard, and dropped it on the desk.
Malia's hand shot up.
"We're still supposed to do it,"
she said.
"Are we?"
said Mr.
Ballard.
"Yes,"
said Malia.
"Because Mrs.
Okafor is going to check."
Mr.
Ballard looked at her for a second with his head tipped over.
Then he said, "You are absolutely right and I respect you enormously.
Get your books."
But he did not teach it the way it was written.
He drew a giant rectangle on the board that took up the whole thing.
"Seven rows,"
he said, drawing lines.
"Eight in each row."
He was drawing far too fast and the lines were crooked.
"How many little boxes?"
Nobody knew.
"Nobody knows!
Excellent!
Count them."
And then he actually made them count all fifty-six out loud, together, pointing at each one, which took a very long time.
It was ridiculous.
Malia counted along and thought about how far behind they were getting.
But when they hit fifty-six, something odd happened.
The number felt different than it had felt before.
It was not a fact she had failed to memorize.
It was a rectangle she had personally counted.
Around her, other kids were saying "ohhh"
in a way she did not usually hear in this room.
Then Mr.
Ballard rubbed out one row with his sleeve, which got chalk all over the pineapple tie.
"Six rows now,"
he said.
"How many?"
Malia's hand went up before she decided to put it up.
"Forty-eight."
"HOW,"
said Mr.
Ballard, delighted again.
"You took away one row, so you took away eight."
Mr.
Ballard put down the eraser and pointed at her with both hands.
"That,"
he said, "is the entire subject.
That right there."
They did not finish pages 40 to 42.
They finished page 40 and about half of 41.
At the end of the day the room looked like something had exploded in it.
There was chalk on the floor.
The chair was still lying on its back.
Malia stayed behind to straighten the desks because she could not stand leaving them crooked, and Mr.
Ballard helped her, badly.
"You are worried I have ruined your class,"
he said.
Malia said, "A little bit."
He nodded, as if that were fair.
"Here is the thing,"
he said.
"You already knew seven eights.
You just did not believe it.
Those are different problems and they need different medicine."
Malia thought about that.
She had known it.
She had gotten it right on a test in September and then decided she was bad at it anyway.
The next morning Mrs.
Okafor was back, and everything was normal, and the chair was upright.
She looked at the board, where a faint crooked rectangle was still showing through the erased chalk.
"What is this?"
she asked.
Twenty-two kids started talking at once.
Mrs.
Okafor listened for a while with a strange look on her face.
Then she got a piece of chalk and drew a rectangle underneath it, neatly, and said, "Nine rows.
Seven in each."
Malia had Mr.
Ballard again in March, for two days, when Mrs.
Okafor had a wedding.
He did not remember her name.
He called her "the one who runs the place,"
which she decided to take as a compliment.
He knocked over the chair again within four minutes.
Malia had already moved her pencil case out of the way, because this time she knew what was coming, and honestly she was looking forward to it.

checks.q: How does Malia feel at the start of the day?
o: Worried, because things are not going normally
checks.why: She likes things to go normally, and the text says her stomach tightened.

checks.q: Why does Malia raise her hand about the folder?
o: Mrs. Okafor is going to check the work
checks.why: She says it directly — they still have to do it because Mrs. Okafor will check.

checks.q: Why does counting all 56 boxes change things for Malia?
o: It stopped being a fact she failed to memorize and became something she counted
checks.why: The number felt different because she had personally counted the rectangle.

checks.q: How does Malia work out 6 rows of 8?
o: She took away one row, which is eight less than 56
checks.why: She explains it herself: one row fewer means eight fewer, so 56 − 8 = 48.

checks.q: What does Mr. Ballard mean about "different medicine"?
o: Not knowing something and not believing it are different problems
She needs to see a doctor
checks.why: He says she already knew it — the problem was that she didn't believe it, which needs fixing differently.

checks.q: Why does Mrs. Okafor draw her own rectangle?
o: She sees that it worked, and uses it herself
checks.why: Inference. She listens to the class, gets a strange look, then copies the method neatly.

words: A person who fills in for someone else.
So silly it is almost funny.
To learn something so you can say it without looking.
